name: Young Stitchers
character: Bright, sturdy, and forgiving: a quilt club for ages 8 to 18 where pins are optional and finished beats perfect.

sections.eyebrow: A quilt club for ages 8 to 18
sections.title: {{guild_name}}
sections.subtitle: Sample text — replace me: We meet after school on Thursdays to sew by hand and by machine, and every member finishes at least one quilt a year.

items.title: Pillowcase season
items.body: Straight seams, no patterns, and everyone takes a finished pillowcase home in October.

items.title: Rag-quilt winter
items.body: Flannel, snipping, and no seam allowances to fuss about while the snow falls.

items.title: The spring group quilt
items.body: Every member pieces one block. We raffle the finished quilt at the school fair.

items.title: Summer sew days
items.body: One long Saturday a month at the library, with a new skill each time.

sections.heading: Where we meet
sections.note: The club owns six machines that live in the cabinet, so nobody has to carry one on the bus.

sections.title: Dues are ten dollars a year
sections.body: That covers fabric, thread, and machine oil. Nobody is turned away; ask us quietly and it is covered.

sections.title: About the club
sections.subtitle: Sample text — replace me: Two grandmothers, one 4-H agent, and a borrowed church basement in 2016. The basement still smells like ironing starch.

sections.heading: What members learn
sections.html:
How to thread a needle and a machine, how to press instead of iron, how to read a cutting mat, and how to unpick a seam without losing patience. The quilt skills are the excuse; the quiet confidence of finishing something real is the point.

Older members mentor younger ones from the first night. A fourteen-year-old who taught a nine-year-old to tie a quilter's knot last spring is now known, accurately, as Professor Knot.

items.quote: My daughter unpicked her own mistake, fixed it, and then explained it to me at dinner like it was nothing.
items.author: A relieved parent

items.quote: I made a quilt for my bed and one for my cousin and the raffle quilt at school is next.
items.author: Priya, age 11

sections.title: Meetings
sections.subtitle: Sample text — replace me: Thursday afternoons during the school year, one long Saturday a month in summer. Snacks at four.

sections.heading: What to bring
sections.html: Just yourself the first time. After that: your project bag, your pins if you have a favorite kind, and any fabric you have been saving. Scissors, machines, irons, and band-aids belong to the club.

sections.title: What we sew
sections.subtitle: Sample text — replace me: One finished thing per season, each one a little harder than the last, by choice.

items.title: Pillowcase
items.body: The starter. One straight seam, one french seam, done in an hour.

items.title: Rag quilt
items.body: Flannel squares, clipped seams, and the dryer does the decorating.

items.title: Nine-patch tote
items.body: Piecing with a purpose, plus straps that survive library books.

items.title: Strip quilt
items.body: The first real quilt, tied with yarn, labeled with a permanent pen.

items.title: Applique banner
items.body: Shapes cut from felt and stitched down for the club booth.

items.title: Free choice
items.body: Mentors on call, machines reserved, and a plan written on the whiteboard.

sections.title: What we finished
sections.subtitle: Sample text — replace me: Every quilt here went home with its maker, and most of them are already on a bed.

sections.heading: About the photos
sections.html: Every face on this page belongs to a member whose grown-up signed the permission slip. Quilts are photographed with first names or no names, whichever the family chose.

sections.title: For parents and guardians
sections.subtitle: Sample text — replace me: Safety, supervision, pickup times, and where the raffle quilt money goes.

sections.heading: The practical details
sections.html:
Every meeting has at least three background-checked adults, including one certified in first aid. Rotary cutters live in a locked drawer and are introduced one skill at a time; the iron is hot and the rule about walking past it is absolute.

Dues are ten dollars for the year and materials are included. The spring raffle quilt is licensed through the county 4-H office and the proceeds buy fabric, thread, and the club's machines; the ledger is read at the family potluck in May.

items.q: My child is 7. Can they join?
items.a: The club starts at 8, but a younger visitor may come with their grown-up and sew at the hand-stitching table.

items.q: Do we need a sewing machine?
items.a: No. The club owns six, and learning to share a machine is part of the first year.
Ten dollars a year, with fabric and thread provided. If the ten dollars is a problem, say so quietly and it is handled.

items.q: What if we miss a meeting?
items.a: Come back anyway. Projects wait patiently in labeled bags, and no step is ever only taught once.

sections.title: Contact the club
sections.subtitle: Sample text — replace me: Registration, visiting before joining, fabric donations, and adults who would like to help.

sections.heading: Donations
sections.html: The club sews through about forty yards of cotton a season and is always glad of clean fabric, especially flannel. Biggest wish right now: safety pins, for basting the spring quilt.
